scope: Batches 07–08, 20 meanings and 60 offline question bands

items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 89:34, mi-jambe means halfway up the leg. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Compared the mid-leg water-height sense with the Académie 4th- and 8th-edition entries for mi and jambe; choices keep the same à mi- compound frame.

items.meaning: to make someone realize; point out
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 94:19, sentir means to make someone realize; point out. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. This causative phrase conveys an argument to the listener, not a physical touch. Linked the published mental-perception sense.

items.meaning: apparent magnitude; a star’s brightness class
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 94:163, grandeur means apparent magnitude; a star’s brightness class. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Grandeur in étoile de la cinquantième grandeur describes stellar apparent brightness class, not physical size; kept four feminine singular noun options.

In chapter IV 94:187, très-distinctement means very clearly; quite distinctly. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 94:292, tâté means felt by touch; palpated. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 94:338, senti means felt; sensed by touch. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The reply vous avez mal senti refers to failed sensory perception; it remains distinct from the figurative faire sentir.

In chapter IV 95:24, globe-ci means this globe here. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The proximal -ci identifies this particular globe; its planned planet sense is shared with the earlier globe route.

In chapter IV 95:44, construit means constructed; put together. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 95:67, irrégulier means irregular; lacking a regular pattern. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Both source uses refer to irregular form or arrangement and have one shared meaning and question set.

In chapter IV 95:150, chaos means chaos; disorder. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 95:180, ruisseaux means small streams; brooks. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 95:225, étangs means ponds; still bodies of water. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The tiny-pond description is the Saturnian’s scale comparison with Earth’s waters; the answer retains the narrator’s noun.

In chapter IV 95:247, ronds means round; circular. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Kept all Level 4–5 shape adjectives masculine plural to agree with étangs and linked the existing round sense.

In chapter IV 95:257, carrés means square; four-sided. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Four-sided alternatives are all masculine plural; only carrés describes four equal sides and right angles.

In chapter IV 95:268, ovales means oval; egg-shaped. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. All unchanged-sentence alternatives agree in masculine plural; an oval is rounded and elongated.

In chapter IV 95:297, régulière means regular; orderly in shape. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. All Level 4–5 adjective choices agree with feminine singular forme.

In chapter IV 95:332, pointus means pointed; sharp-tipped. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. All Level 4–5 adjective choices agree with masculine plural grains.

In chapter IV 95:358, hérissé means bristling; studded with points. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. The source context and each three-band contrast were checked for the target meaning, agreement and one intended answer.

In chapter IV 95:380, écorché means scraped; abraded the skin. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Changed the middle sentence to keep the object after the auxiliary, so all four uninflected past-participle choices are grammatical.

items.meaning: the poles; ends of Earth’s axis
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 96:71, pôles means the poles; ends of Earth’s axis. The questions contrast this contextual sense and preserve its source use. Both source uses mean the Earth’s geographic poles, and the noun alternatives are masculine plurals.
